title: The Immaculate Conception (8 December)
hook: readings from Genesis 3 and the Annunciation
carry: full of grace from the start

segments.voice: Yesterday, Advent with Isaiah, and a line for the long nights: a great light. Did you notice the first light you switched on after dark? Day six hundred thirty-five.

Ask a room of people what the Immaculate Conception is, and a good half will say: it's when Jesus was conceived without a human father. It's one of the most common mix-ups in Catholic vocabulary, and it's an easy one to make. But that's the virgin birth, a different teaching. December 8 is about Mary herself, and about the first moment of her own life. In the middle of Advent, nine months before her birthday on September 8, the Church stops for a solemnity. And the readings it chooses go all the way back to a garden.
screen: `NOT THE VIRGIN BIRTH.` → `MARY'S OWN BEGINNING.` → `BACK TO A GARDEN.`

segments.voice: The first reading is Genesis 3. Adam and Eve have eaten the fruit and hidden. God walks in the garden and calls, where art thou? Then God speaks to the serpent, in the Douay-Rheims: "I will put enmities between thee and the woman, and thy seed and her seed: she shall crush thy head." She, in that translation, because the Latin Vulgate says ipsa. The Hebrew points instead to the woman's offspring, he or it. Either way, Christians have long heard in this verse a first promise: a woman and her child, and a struggle with evil that ends in victory. Then the gospel jumps to Nazareth. The angel Gabriel greets a young woman: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee." Full of grace translates one Greek word, kecharitōmenē, a form that suggests favor already given and still lasting. In 1854, Pope Pius IX defined what Catholics had long celebrated: that Mary, from the first instant of her conception, was kept free of original sin, by a singular grace, in view of what her son would do. Not because she earned it, and not apart from Christ, but as the first fruit of his work. Put the two readings side by side and the shape appears: Eve, who said no in the garden, and Mary, who would say yes in Nazareth. Christian traditions differ here. Orthodox Christians honor Mary as all-holy but generally don't accept the teaching in this defined form, and most Protestants don't hold it. For Catholics it's a holy day, and in the United States, Mary under this title is the nation's patroness.
screen: `GENESIS 3: SHE SHALL CRUSH.` · `HAIL, FULL OF GRACE.` · `1854: FREE FROM THE FIRST INSTANT.` · `EVE'S NO, MARY'S YES.` · then, large: `FULL OF GRACE FROM THE START.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one Hail Mary, slowly. If you pray, say it once, aloud or silently. It opens with the angel's own greeting, and then Elizabeth's, before it asks anything. Let each phrase land before the next. If you don't pray, sit with the angel's greeting itself, full of grace, and think of a beginning in your own life that was a gift, something you didn't earn. Then rest in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
The Immaculate Conception. The Catholic teaching that Mary was kept free from original sin from the first moment of her life, kept on December 8. Today's word.
Your line: full of grace from the start. Today, if someone mixes up the Immaculate Conception and the virgin birth, you'll know the difference. Day six hundred thirty-five.

howItsDone: Catholics keep December 8 as a solemnity, a holy day of obligation in many countries, with readings from Genesis 3 and Luke's account of the Annunciation.

fork.setup: you're Mary in Nazareth. an angel appears and says, hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee. what do you do first?
options: bow at once and say yes.
feel troubled, and wonder what this greeting means.
fork.reveal: Luke says she was troubled and wondered what manner of greeting this could be. her yes comes later, after her own question.

original.note: Greek: full of grace, favored one; the angel's name for Mary in Luke 1:28.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Immaculate Conception is the virgin birth.
what it means: Mary was kept free of original sin from her own conception, celebrated on December 8.
what a scholar hears: defined by Pius IX in 1854 (Ineffabilis Deus); the readings pair Genesis 3:15, where the Vulgate reads ipsa, with the angel's kecharitōmenē.
